H1.text: Jump onto concrete, and it jars your knees. Jump into a sand pit, and it feels soft.

H2.text: A fielder pulls his hands back as he catches. Same ball, same speed. So what changes?

H3.text: Diya has a kitchen challenge. Catch a raw egg, tossed across the room, without breaking it.

H4.text: Stiff hands, and it cracks. Hands that move back with it, and it survives. Why?

H5.text: The egg must lose the same momentum either way. The secret is the time.

P1.text: That idea has a name. Impulse.

P2.text: Last episode, force was the rate of change of momentum. F equals change in p over change in t.

P3.text: Multiply both sides by the time. F times delta t equals delta p.

P4.text: F times delta t is called the impulse, J. So impulse equals the change in momentum.

P5.text: Its unit is the newton second, the same as a kilogram metre per second.

S1.text: To the motion notebook. Two clay balls of two hundred grams, at five metres per second. Clay does not bounce.

S2.text: The first hits a hard wall, and stops in two hundredths of a second.

S3.text: In slow motion, the force shoots up to almost eighty newtons, then falls away. A tall, thin spike.

S4.text: The second hits a soft cushion. It takes eight hundredths of a second to stop.

S5.text: Now the force peaks at only about twenty newtons. A low, wide hump.

S6.text: Now compare the areas. Both are one newton second. Each ball lost the same momentum.

S7.text: Four times the time, a quarter of the average force. Fifty newtons, against twelve and a half.

D1.text: Let's write it in small steps.

D2.text: Step one. The change in momentum is final minus initial. Delta p equals m v minus m u.

D3.text: Step two. For a steady force, J equals F delta t, which equals delta p.

D4.text: Step three. When the force changes, J is the area under the force time graph.

D5.text: Step four. For a clay ball, delta p is zero minus one, so minus one newton second. The minus means the force points back.

D6.text: Step five. Average force is delta p over delta t. Same delta p, longer time, smaller force.

T1.text: Remember this. Impulse equals change in momentum. Stretch the time, and the force shrinks.

K1.text: Side by side, with Diya's egg. Sixty grams, at five metres per second. It must lose zero point three newton seconds.

K2.text: Stiff hands stop it in one hundredth of a second. Thirty newtons, a sharp jolt.

K3.text: Soft hands move back, and take a tenth of a second. Just three newtons.

K4.text: Now you try. Which catch gives the egg the bigger impulse? Pause and decide.

K5.text: The same! Both catches take away the same momentum. Only the force differs, because the time differs.

G2.text: A long jumper lands in sand. Wrestlers fall on thick mats.

G3.text: Car airbags and crumple zones stretch a crash over a longer time.

G4.text: And you bend your knees when you land. Each one makes delta t longer, so the force is smaller.

G5.text: Your turn. Why does a high jumper land on a thick foam bed? Pause and decide.

G6.text: A longer stopping time! The momentum to lose is the same. The foam spreads it over more time.

W2.text: A one hundred and fifty gram ball reaches a fielder at twenty metres per second. He stops it in zero point one seconds. Find the impulse and the force.

W3.text: Delta p is zero, minus zero point one five times twenty. Minus three newton seconds.

W4.text: So the impulse on the ball is three newton seconds, against its motion.

W5.text: The average force is three over zero point one. Thirty newtons.

W6.text: With stiff hands, in zero point zero two seconds, it would be one hundred and fifty newtons.

X2.text: A ball hits a wall at ten metres per second, and bounces back at ten. Many say the momentum did not change.

X3.text: But velocity is a vector. Plus ten became minus ten. So delta p is minus twenty m. Its size is two m v.

E1.text: Where is this asked? In force time graphs, and in bounce and catch questions.

Q1.text: Exam level now. A half kilogram ball falls from five metres onto a floor, and bounces up to one point eight metres. The contact lasts zero point one seconds. Take g as ten. Find the average force from the floor. Pause and solve.

A1.text: The answer is C. Eighty five newtons.

A2.text: It hits the floor at ten metres per second, down. It leaves at six, up. Take up as positive.

A3.text: Delta p is half, times six minus minus ten. Eight newton seconds, upward.

A4.text: So the net force is eighty newtons. The floor must also hold up the weight, five newtons. Eighty five.

F1.text: Here is your recap. Screenshot this card.

Y1.text: Can you answer these without help?

Y2.text: One. What is impulse, and what is its unit?

Y3.text: Two. Why does a fielder pull his hands back?

Y4.text: Three. A ball bounces back at the same speed. Why is delta p not zero?

N1.text: Next time: two carts at rest push apart. Where does their momentum come from? Conservation of linear momentum.
